title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
text:
The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.
The Transformation of the U.S. Oil Sector
The U.S. economy has a history of being vulnerable to geopolitical developments. Domestic drilling stopped rising in 1970, meaning that increases in consumption had to be satisfied by imports, which doubled from 1970 to 1973. Most of this new supply was from OPEC and the 1973 crisis illustrated how domestic gasoline prices could rise dramatically because of foreign developments. This point was reinforced by another price shock in 1979.
This vulnerability led to the creation of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), a government stockpile to be released when oil supplies were threatened, but little else could be done about the underlying trend. In the years that followed, the rise in oil demand, coupled with stagnant drilling, caused imports to exceed exports by 9 million barrels per day (mb/d) in 2010, or almost half of domestic consumption.
The situation changed with the adoption of fracking technology. As seen in the chart below, U.S. output of crude oil and other liquid fuels jumped from 8 mb/d in 2010 to 21 mb/d in 2025. To put the increase in perspective, global production rose by 19 mb/d over this period, meaning the United States accounted for 70 percent of that gain.
U.S. Production Has Increased Dramatically
A key development behind the sustained production surge was the 2015 repeal of a 1975 law that had largely prohibited exports of crude oil. (Exports of refined products were not restricted.) The industry successfully argued that the potential output from the Permian Basin in New Mexico and Texas was more than the Gulf region’s refineries could accommodate. Its recommended solution to this bottleneck was to permit selling into foreign markets. Consumers would benefit, even if the added oil was exported, as the boost to global production would feed back into lower domestic prices.
The chart below shows how the 2015 repeal affected trade flows. From 2010 to 2015, the increase in drilling reduced imports of crude liquids and refined products and increased exports by roughly equal amounts (2 mb/d). But with the end of restrictions on crude oil sales, petroleum exports increased by an additional 6 mb/d from 2015 to 2025, while imports fell by 2 mb/d.
U.S. Petroleum Exports Now Exceed Imports
A Sudden Shortage After Being Oversupplied
The conflict with Iran severely disrupted the petroleum market. The chart below shows the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s (EIA) estimate of global production of liquid fuels and global consumption. The change in inventory levels is the gap between the production (supply) and consumption (demand) lines based on the market clearing equation:
Supply + Change in Inventories = Demand
For example, the last observation for September puts production at 101 mb/d and demand at 104 mb/d, implying inventory levels declined at a rate of 3 mb/d in the month.
Inventories Were Growing Before Hostilities Started
Supply moved substantially above demand over the course of 2025, as higher output in the United States, Brazil, and others increased production while demand rose more slowly. Consequently, inventories went from being unchanged in 2024 to rising at a 2 mb/d average rate in 2025 and at a 4 mb/d rate in the first two months of 2026. Global production collapsed by 12 mb/d in March, so having this oversupply significantly reduced the amount of the shortfall that had to be made up.
The gap between supply and demand caused inventories to fall at a rate of 5 mb/d in March. Similar drawdowns happened in April and May before output recovered in June when tensions eased, leaving inventories shrinking at a 3.5 mb/d rate in the second quarter. Inventories stabilized in July, but the resumption of tensions caused inventory levels to fall at a 3 mb/d rate in August and September.
Running Down the Buffer
How did the U.S. oil sector help bridge the supply shortfall? The options were either to increase production or to draw down inventories. There was not much that could be done immediately on the production side as the industry does not operate with spare capacity. Drilling is growing but at a rate similar to rates achieved in recent years, with the EIA forecasting U.S output rising by 0.7 mb/d in 2026 versus 0.9 mb/d in 2024 and 2025.
That left domestic inventories. Their level was unchanged in March but then fell in the next three months, with the SPR releasing crude oil at the rate of 1 mb/d in the second quarter and commercial inventories falling at a 0.7 mb/d rate. Together this drawdown accounted for roughly half of the estimated drop in global inventory levels.
The decline in inventories, along with modest changes in drilling and consumption, translated into more oil available for the rest of the world. In terms of trade flows, net exports increased by 2.5 mb/d in the second quarter, with exports up 2 mb/d and imports down by 0.5 mb/d.
U.S. inventories stopped falling in July, as seen in the chart below, and remained relatively flat through September. The end of the drawdown caused the net exports balance in the third quarter to fall back to near its first quarter level.

title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
text:
Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper, we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender’s funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.
Credit Card Lenders Serve Many Different Markets
Credit card lenders do not compete in a single, undifferentiated national market. They target offers and design products for particular types of borrowers. Industry reports, regulatory guidance, and academic research document segmentation by credit risk, income, card characteristics, and acquisition channel. A prime borrower applying online for a general-purpose, non-co-branded card belongs to a different market than a subprime borrower accepting a preapproved offer for a general-purpose, co-branded card. The same lender can have a large share in one of these markets and a small share in another.
Guided by these documented practices, we define 960 nationwide markets by combining four credit-score groups, card and product type, acquisition channel, and income groups based on the borrower’s ZIP code. In our data, lenders operate in about 200 of these markets on average in a given week. Within each market, we define a lender’s share as its revenue relative to total revenue in that market.
Rates Track Lenders’ Market Position
We begin by asking whether the rates borrowers receive are related to their lender’s share of the market. To do so, we use confidential account-level data collected by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). The data report annual percentage rates (APRs) and detailed borrower and card characteristics for newly issued accounts. We form groups of accounts finely matched on observed borrower and product characteristics, such as income, credit score, and credit card type, so that the accounts within any group look much alike.
The chart below plots the average APR in each group (vertical axis) against the average market share of the lenders issuing those cards (horizontal axis). The relation is clearly positive, with a correlation of 54 percent: higher lender market shares are associated with higher APRs. In the companion paper, we show this is not driven by differences in characteristics across borrowers (for example, default risk) or across banks (for example, lending costs); market shares remain strongly related to rates once those characteristics are accounted for.
Credit Card Rates Are Tied to a Lenders’ Market Share
Group averages, though, can still differ for reasons other than market positions. For instance, groups vary in default risk, and riskier borrowers pay a higher APR. For that reason, in the companion paper we examine differences in APRs within each group, where credit score, income, and credit card type are held fixed by construction, so differences in rates within a group cannot be attributed to them. We find that, even among borrowers and cards that look very similar in the data, differences in APRs are larger when differences in lenders’ market positions are larger.
While these patterns are suggestive, they remain descriptive. Lenders may hold large shares in markets that differ in ways we do not observe, and those differences could also affect APRs. We therefore turn to a more direct test of lender conduct.
What Happens When Lenders’ Funding Costs Fall?
Most variable-rate credit card accounts are tied to a contractual benchmark after they are issued, so changes in APRs on existing accounts are partly mechanical. We instead study accounts at origination, when the lender chooses the initial APR, including its spread over that benchmark.
Our baseline analysis focuses on January 2008 since it had one of the largest unanticipated movements in the federal funds rate. For additional events through 2019, we supplement this data with comparable information collected by the Federal Reserve. Together, the two datasets cover roughly 14 million newly issued accounts and report their origination dates, APRs, and detailed borrower and card characteristics.
When an unexpected change in the risk-free rate moves lenders’ cost of funds, we compare accounts issued shortly before and shortly after the change. We strip out APR changes common to all of a lender’s markets and adjust for observed differences in borrowers and products, including credit score, income, and card type. What remains is a comparison of the same lender, around the same unexpected change in the risk-free rate, across markets where its share differs. We refer to the resulting measure as the adjusted APR.
Consider a lender that has a large share in one market but a small share in another, and suppose the risk-free rate declines by 25 basis points. If the lender passed the decline through fully in both markets, APRs on newly issued accounts would fall by 25 basis points in each. Instead, suppose it cuts APRs by 15 basis points in the high-share market and by 20 basis points in the low-share market. The difference between these responses measures how much less of the decline is passed through where the lender has a larger share.
Lenders Pass Through Less Where Their Shares Are Larger
Our clearest evidence comes from January 2008, when the federal funds rate fell unexpectedly by 25 basis points. We compare how the same lender adjusts its rates in its high-share markets versus its low-share markets, in the weeks right around the unexpected fed funds rate change. title: Christine Lagarde: Interview with Yomiuri Shimbun
text:
- INTERVIEW
Interview with Yomiuri Shimbun
Interview with Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, conducted by Hironari Akiyama on 4 November 2026
7 November 2026
On the glass ceiling and women in power – could you share your own experiences for Japanese women, not least because you know their situation as well?
I discussed this topic a lot with Prime Minister Abe and his wife. He was determined to make a change for Japan at the time, and he had this programme called “One Million Women”. He got one million additional women into the workplace by implementing quite a few policies that were really helpful, like giving more freedom to the municipalities to open childcare centres.
So thanks to Prime Minister Abe things changed a lot. And it helped women access positions of professional responsibility.
At the ECB you became the first female leader. Did you have any difficulties or challenges in terms of being the first woman to lead the ECB?
It’s always challenging to be in a minority. In Governing Council meetings, when I look around the table, there are 27 people seated, and only two women. So that’s definitely a minority. Isabel Schnabel, who is a Member of the Executive Board and who is stepping down at the beginning of January, and me. So just two. It’s always a challenge when you’re a minority, but I think when you reach that sort of high level, because you are the President, people have to accept that, because it’s a matter of institutional strength and it’s a matter of governance as well. But it’s challenging, yes, of course.
But the situation has not changed from seven years ago. I mean, seven years ago, there was...
There was one single woman.
What do you think? Why did this happen?
Those decisions are made by the governments of the Member States and, typically, governments go for a man. First of all, because I think that while the pipeline of talented women is building up, this is only a recent development. And second, because people tend to choose other people who look like them. So you have many men in government, and they tend to appoint other men.
I want to ask about monetary policy. Sorry to change to a serious question. How do you see the inflation outlook now?
The other one was serious as well. Both questions are serious.
Headline inflation in October was at 4%, which was higher than we had expected a few months ago but in line with market expectations. It looks very high. But it’s important to look under the hood.
It’s largely attributable to energy, because energy inflation increased to 20.8%, up from 18.9% in September, driven by the conflict in the Middle East and less global refinery capacity. So energy is weighing heavily on our inflation numbers. Food inflation has also increased.
But the underlying indicators are stable. Core inflation, taking out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.5%, unchanged from September. Services inflation edged up a little to 3.3% but remains in the range we have seen over the last four months.
We still don’t have the detailed inflation breakdown, which will shed more light on what’s driving services inflation – that is, whether it’s mainly very energy intensive sectors like transport or whether we are starting to see broader indirect effects. We’ll look closely at this.
In any event, we know that inflation numbers will remain high in the quarters to come. The higher they are, and the longer they remain high, the greater the risk to our medium-term target.
How about second-round effects? Are they still limited?
Yes. We are currently not seeing signs of second-round effects beyond what we have incorporated in our projections. We’re watching carefully the forward-looking indicators – multi-year wage agreements, companies’ wage expectations – and we don’t see evidence of a shift yet.
I understand, but can we expect you to revise the projections upwards because inflation is at 4%?
I don’t think it’s appropriate to pre-empt the forecast. But clearly there have been some important changes since our September projections. Energy futures curves are higher, which will have a bearing on both inflation and growth, although oil prices have come down more recently. Long-term interest rates are also higher. Our forecast exercise will determine how these different forces affect medium-term inflation.
Looking back to 2021, to the energy shock and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, some people have pointed out that the ECB was behind the curve.
Yes. I know
It’s so important for Japanese people to know what you learnt about that.
It’s not something that was specific to Europe, but to all of us. I remember vividly the discussions we had at the Bank for International Settlements, and everybody from the Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan, the ECB, we all assessed that we were facing a supply shock that was going to be transitory. As a result we decided that it was appropriate to look through it and let supply-driven inflation come back down, just as it had gone up. That was, in hindsight, misguided because the situation was much more complicated. There was a demand shock happening at the same time as the economy reopened and consumers spending their built-up savings. So that led us all to revisit our assumption that it was all transitory.
So, learning from this, do you think there is a need for an interest rate hike before any secondary effects become apparent?
I think what we have experienced recently, and are still experiencing, massively, is uncertainty. Unpredictability. The fragmentation of the world as we knew it. Trade disruptions, supply chain disruptions, and a focus on security more than efficiency – all of that is completely changing the landscape in which economic players are operating. And as a result of that situation, we have established that we will decide our monetary policy on the basis of data and meeting by meeting.

title: ECB publishes consolidated banking data for end-June 2026
text:
- PRESS RELEASE
ECB publishes consolidated banking data for end-June 2026
6 November 2026
- The aggregate of total assets of EU-headquartered credit institutions increased by 5.18%, from €33.27 trillion in June 2025 to €34.99 trillion in June 2026
- During the same period, EU credit institutions’ aggregate non-performing loans ratio[1] increased by 0.03 percentage points year on year to stand at 1.99% in June 2026
- EU credit institutions’ aggregate return on equity[2] was 5.31% in June 2026 and their Common Equity Tier 1 ratio[3] was 16.43%
Chart 1
Total assets of credit institutions headquartered in the EU
Chart 2
Non-performing loans ratio of credit institutions headquartered in the EU
Chart 3
Return on equity of credit institutions headquartered in the EU in June 2026
Chart 4
Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of credit institutions headquartered in the EU in June 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) has published consolidated banking data as at end-June 2026, a dataset for the EU banking system compiled on a group consolidated basis.
The quarterly data provide information required to analyse the EU banking sector and comprise a subset of the information that is available in the year-end dataset. The data cover 336 banking groups and 2283 stand-alone credit institutions and non-EU controlled subsidiaries and branches operating in the EU, accounting for nearly 100% of the EU banking sector’s balance sheet. They include an extensive range of indicators on profitability and efficiency, balance sheet composition, liquidity and funding, asset quality, asset encumbrance, capital adequacy and solvency. Aggregates and indicators are published for the reporting population.
Reporters generally apply International Financial Reporting Standards and the European Banking Authority’s Implementing Technical Standards on Supervisory Reporting. However, some small and medium-sized reporters may apply national accounting standards. Accordingly, aggregates and indicators may include some data that are based on national accounting standards, depending on the availability of the underlying items.
In addition to data as of end-June 2026, the published figures also include a few revisions to past data.
For media queries, please contact Benoit Deeg, tel.: +491721683704.
Notes
- These consolidated banking data are available in the ECB Data Portal.
- More information about the methodology used to compile the data is available on the ECB's website.
- Hyperlinks in the main body of the press release lead to data that may change with subsequent releases as a result of revisions.
- Defined as the ratio of non-performing loans to total loans. Cash balances at central banks and other demand deposits are included.
- Defined as the ratio of total profit (loss) for the first six months of 2026 (non-annualised) to total equity. Profitability indicators are not annualised.
- Defined as the ratio of Common Equity Tier 1 capital to the total risk exposure amount.

title: Data and analytics transformation at the Bank of England to enable, equip and empower − speech by Ben Martin
text:
Speech
Good morning. It is a great pleasure to be here today at the DAMA Data & AI Conference. This event is about sharing practical experience of building trusted, responsible and effective data and AI capabilities, so I thought it would be a good opportunity to share some of the work we are doing on this at the Bank of England.
In recent years, my colleagues at the Bank have spoken publicly about the implications of AI on the wider economyfootnote [1] footnote [2]. Today, I want to talk about this from a slightly different perspective: what data and analytics transformation means for the Bank of England itself, as an organisation.
But first, let me introduce myself: my name is Ben Martin and I am the Bank’s Chief Data Officer. I took up this role just under a year ago, following a career across the Bank’s economics, markets and supervision areas. This experience gave me a deep understanding of the Bank’s data needs. Taking on the CDO role has allowed me to bring those perspectives together at an enterprise level. It has been encouraging to see how much progress we have made – and continue to make – in improving our data, analytics and AI capabilities. Even though we are making good progress, this is by no means job done. The pace of change in this field is rapid, and our ambitions need to keep pace with it. So today, I want to reflect on the journey we have been on, where we are now, and some of the opportunities and challenges that lie ahead.
Our mission at the Bank of England is to promote the good of the people of the United Kingdom, by maintaining monetary and financial stability. Across our offices in London and Leeds, our people are working to deliver that mission. Central to this is our ability to make the best possible decisions using the most effective data and analytics to achieve our public policy objectives. Data and analytics are integral to our work. They support our understanding of the economy, our supervision of the financial firms within it, and the operations through which we fulfil our responsibilities.
A couple of years ago, we published our Data & Analytics Strategyfootnote [3]. Our overarching aim is to make the best use of data and analytics to fulfil the Bank’s mission. Our ambitions are summarised by three missions.
- First, making it easy for people in the Bank to work with and analyse data.
- Second, bridging data gaps to increase the value of what we collect and share.
- Third, enabling safe and effective innovation, including artificial intelligence.
Those missions rest on two foundations: a modern enterprise data platform on the cloud; and investment in business change, skills and culture to embed this.
That combination is important. We are not simply replacing systems. We are seeking to change how people find and use data, how they collaborate on it with each other, and how they develop new analytical tools and techniques to gain the best insights to make good decisions.
Today I want to focus on how we are enabling, equipping and empowering our organisation to deliver this strategy. Let me give a quick overview before we dive into each in more detail later on.
First, what do I mean by enablement? This covers the work we are doing to build solid foundations by providing transformed systems and high-quality data for our colleagues.
Second, we are equipping our colleagues with new capabilities including AI, with effective guardrails and associated training, so they can safely achieve new insights.
Last, but by no means least, I will cover empowerment – our approach to supporting colleagues to make the most of the investment we have made and to have the confidence to explore these new tools.
I am a big fan of the television programme Grand Designs, watching people use exciting, modern solutions in an innovative way to build something truly special – not just special on paper or to look at, but special for the people who live there. I sometimes think about our strategy in the same way. We are using modern techniques and the latest thinking on how to use data, but not as an end in itself or to wow anyone. Instead, the point is to deliver the Bank’s mission effectively and to make sure our colleagues can flourish. We are enabling colleagues by putting the foundations in place, equipping them with new capabilities to continue building on those foundations and empowering them to make the most of those new capabilities. Thankfully, the one thing we don’t have is Kevin McCloud turning up every few months to see how we’re getting on!
I will say a bit more about the work we are doing on these three Es – enable, equip and empower – at the Bank of England.
Enable – by building solid foundations
As I have said, we are building solid foundations, so we can enable our colleagues by providing effective systems and high-quality data as the bedrock of good analysis. At the Bank, we are part way through a multi-year investment programme to build solid data foundations. This includes investing in new systems and technology, but also continuing to invest in the ‘bread and butter’ of good data management: quality, governance and trust. AI may be grabbing the headlines, but AI runs on data. This audience knows well enough that without high-quality, well-governed and trusted data, even the most sophisticated AI will struggle to deliver. So I will share some reflections on how we are bringing together the new systems and the good old basics to ensure solid foundations.
New systems
At the foundation of our Data & Analytics Strategy is a new Enterprise Data Platform, or EDP. This is our central, cloud-based data and analytics ecosystem. It will bring together a wide range of data needed across the Bank’s responsibilities, including macroeconomic and financial market data we bring in from partners, and the regulatory and statistical returns we collect directly from the financial sector. But the EDP is about much more than storing data. It provides a structured and governed way of brin
